paragraphs.heading: Where shells stop surviving
paragraphs.text: The carbonate compensation depth, or CCD, is the depth in the ocean where calcium carbonate dissolves exactly as fast as it arrives from above. Deeper than this, dissolving wins, so the carbonate shells of plankton, called tests, are not kept. On seafloor lying below the CCD, carbonate particles cannot build up in the sediment.

paragraphs.heading: Calcite and aragonite
paragraphs.text: Calcium carbonate comes in more than one crystal form. Calcite is the least soluble of them, so the CCD usually refers to calcite. Aragonite dissolves more easily, so its own compensation depth, the ACD, generally sits shallower.

paragraphs.heading: How the boundary works
paragraphs.text: Living things make calcium carbonate tests near the sunlit surface. When they die, the tests that avoid dissolving near the top sink along with clay. Partway down lies the saturation horizon, a boundary set by temperature, pressure and depth. Above it, the water is supersaturated and tests mostly survive; below it, the water is undersaturated, partly because solubility grows with depth and partly because decaying organic matter releases CO₂, so carbonate dissolves. Debris sinks quickly, so most dissolving happens at the sediment surface. The zone between the saturation horizon and the CCD is called the lysocline.

paragraphs.heading: Chalk above, ooze below
paragraphs.text: Where the seabed lies above the CCD, its sediment can be calcareous ooze, essentially a kind of limestone or chalk, made mostly of Rhizaria. Below the CCD, small carbonate shells dissolve before reaching the bottom. There the most common ooze is siliceous ooze, made mostly of radiolarians and diatoms.

paragraphs.heading: What sets the depth
paragraphs.text: How deep the CCD sits depends on how soluble calcium carbonate is, which in turn depends on temperature, pressure and the water's chemistry, above all its dissolved CO₂. Carbonate dissolves more readily in colder water, under higher pressure and with more dissolved CO₂. Today the CCD lies at about 4200–4500 m in the Pacific, but about 5000 m beneath the equatorial upwelling zone. It sits near 5000 m in the temperate and tropical Atlantic and around 4300 m in the Indian Ocean.

paragraphs.heading: Old water, shallow line
paragraphs.text: The depth varies largely with the age of the water, meaning how long since that deep water last touched the surface. Organic material such as copepod droppings keeps sinking into deep water, so deep water gathers dissolved CO₂ over time. The oldest water therefore has the most CO₂ and the shallowest CCD. Where downwelling sends young, low-CO₂ surface water into the deep, as in the North Atlantic, the CCD is pushed deeper.

paragraphs.heading: A line that moves
paragraphs.text: The CCD has shifted a great deal through geologic time. From the Cretaceous through the Eocene it was much shallower worldwide, when intense volcanic activity had raised atmospheric CO₂. When Earth changed from a greenhouse to an icehouse in the late Eocene, the CCD deepened. Today, burning fossil fuels is raising CO₂ and making the CCD rise, and ocean acidification will make it shallower over tens to hundreds of years.
